newsitem.title: USA: U.N. Iraq sanctions chair sees oil deal renewal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Iraq sanctions chair sees oil deal renewal.

text.p: The chairman of the United Nations sanctions committee on Iraq said Wednesday that the $2 billion "oil-for-food" accord with Baghdad appears on track for renewal in June.

The accord, which has been running since December 10, 1996, is an exception to broader sanctions imposed after Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait and allows $2 billion of oil exports over 180 days to pay for badly needed food, medicines and other essential goods.
A decision on renewal is expected before the end of the current accord on June 7.

Portuguese ambassador Antonio Victor Martins, after reporting to sanctions committee members, told Reuters that "no real problems" were found with the oil sales, while delays in approving food contracts and distrubution currently were being addressed.
"We can favorably look at renewal of 986," Martins said, referring to the U.N. resolution setting out terms of the deal.
The ambassador noted that expedited procedures were adopted by the committee on Wednesday to further speed humanitarian shipments to Iraq.
"We reached agreement to alleviate bureaucratic procedures and to even save some money. It was a very profitable session," he said.

Sanctions members were briefed by two top U.N. officials, including Yohannes Mengesha, director of the Iraq program for the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs, who has recently returned from Iraq.
He said he found Iraqis complying with terms of the oil deal. "Our monitors are doing a good job. We have checked warehouses and all other areas and saw no serious trouble," he said.

Meanwhile, Martins said the structure for reviewing the oil accord was not discussed in the meeting, nor was there any talk of increasing the accord. Though Baghdad officials have at various points said the deal should be increased substantially, there has been no formal request lodged to day.

U.N. undersecretary general Yasushi Akashi, head of the U.N.'s Department of Humanitarian Affairs, will report to the committee next week following his trip last week to Iraq. His conclusions will form part of U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan's broader report to the Security Council which must be delivered before a formal decision can be taken to renew the accord.
